question.text:
You are evaluating the financial health of two automobile companies based on their financial ratios: Company X: Current Ratio = 2.5, Quick Ratio = 1.5 Company Y: Current Ratio = 2.0, Quick Ratio = 1.0
Rank the companies based on liquidity.

answer.text: Both companies have the same liquidity
Cannot determine from the given data

explanation.text: The Logic: Liquidity is read from the Current Ratio (Current Assets / Current Liabilities) and the Quick Ratio ((Current Assets – Inventory) / Current Liabilities). Company X scores higher on both — Current Ratio 2.5 vs 2.0 and Quick Ratio 1.5 vs 1.0 — so X is more liquid than Y. The Trap: Ranking Y ahead of X is the classic mistake of confusing lower ratios with 'leaner working capital'; 'same liquidity' ignores the gap; 'cannot determine' wrongly assumes more line items are needed when two standardised ratios already settle the ranking. Cross-Exam Context: Liquidity-ratio comparisons recur in NISM XV (Investment Adviser) and X-A / X-B (Investment Adviser Levels 1 & 2) under fundamental analysis. Distributor's Pro-Tip: When an HNI asks why a PMS portfolio holds the 'boring' name over the flashy one, show the current and quick ratios side-by-side — it is the simplest one-minute proof that the boring name can actually pay its bills.
